claims.claim: The tau biosensors report changes in tau conformation and self-interaction associated with tau phosphorylation.
claims.source: Our repertoire of tau biosensors reliably reports i. molecular proximity of physiological full-length tau at microtubules; ii. changes in tau conformation and self-interaction associated with tau phosphorylation
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by forskolin-induced phosphorylation experiments showing increased biosensor signals.

claims.claim: The tau biosensors report tau interaction induced by seeds of recombinant tau or from mouse brain lysates of a mouse model of tau pathology.
claims.source: Our repertoire of tau biosensors reliably reports i. molecular proximity of physiological full-length tau at microtubules; ii. changes in tau conformation and self-interaction associated with tau phosphorylation, as well as iii. tau interaction induced by seeds of recombinant tau or from mouse brain lysates of a mouse model of tau pathology.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing biosensor responses to recombinant tau seeds and transgenic mouse brain lysates.

claims.claim: Under physiological conditions, tau is found mainly associated with microtubules (MTs), participating in the regulation of MT assembly/disassembly, with an impact on axonal transport and synapsis structural organization.
claims.source: Under physiological conditions, tau is found mainly associated with microtubules (MTs), participating in the regulation of MT assembly/disassembly, with an impact on axonal transport and synapsis structural organization.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about tau's physiological function.

claims.claim: In AD and other tauopathies, tau undergoes a pathological transformation that involves hyperphosphorylation, conformational changes, loss of MT-binding affinity, and oligomerization, ultimately resulting in tau mislocation and NFTs formation.
claims.source: In AD and other tauopathies, tau undergoes a pathological transformation that involves hyperphosphorylation, conformational changes, loss of MT-binding affinity, and oligomerization, ultimately resulting in tau mislocation and NFTs formation (Ugalde et al., 2016; Goedert, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Progressive accumulation of NFTs in specific brain areas is the molecular marker that mostly correlates with AD cognitive dysfunction and is the basis of the Braak classification of AD into VI stages.
claims.source: Progressive accumulation of NFTs in specific brain areas is the molecular marker that mostly correlates with AD cognitive dysfunction and is the basis of the Braak classification of AD into VI stages (Braak and Braak, 1996).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to the Braak classification system.

claims.claim: Tau is encoded by the MAPT gene and is expressed as six different isoforms due to alternative splicing.
claims.source: Tau is encoded by the MAPT gene and is expressed as six different isoforms due to alternative splicing, referred to as 0N3R, 1N3R, 2N3R, 0N4R, 1N4R, and 2N4R, depending on the presence or absence of two near-amino-terminal inserts (N) and of three (3 R) or four (4 R) repeats in its central repeat domain (Mandelkow and Mandelkow, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about tau isoforms supported by citation.

claims.claim: All tau isoforms except 0N3R are expressed in the human brain and all can be found in aggregates observed in AD brains.
claims.source: Except for the 0N3R isoform, which is found only in newborns, all the other isoforms are expressed in the human brain and all can be found in aggregates observed in AD brains.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about tau isoform expression and aggregation.

claims.claim: Tau pathology is propagated and spread between neurons in a prion-like mechanism, transmitting the misfolded pathological conformation to other native tau molecules through a prion-like seeding effect.
claims.source: Once started, tau pathology is propagated and spread between neurons in a prion-like mechanism, transmitting the misfolded pathological conformation to other native tau molecules through a prion-like seeding effect (Iba et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature on tau propagation.

claims.claim: HEK293T cells expressing a fixed amount of LgBit-K18(P301L) and increasing amounts of SmBit-K18(P301L) showed a saturation profile of the complementation signal.
claims.source: HEK293T cells expressing a fixed amount of LgBit-K18(P301L) and increasing amounts of SmBit-K18(P301L), showed the expected saturation profile of the complementation signal, reflecting specific interaction and progressive saturation of LgBit-K18(P301L) with SmBit-K18(P301L) (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: The K18(P301L) biosensor showed a punctuated staining pattern predominantly in the cytosol with some co-localization with tubulin as well as some nuclear staining.
claims.source: The K18(P301L) biosensor showed a punctuated staining pattern predominantly in the cytosol with some co-localization with tubulin as well as some nuclear staining (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: A robust increase in signal was observed in K18(P301L) sensor-expressing cells treated for 24 hr with either monomeric K18 (mK18) or aggK18.
claims.source: A robust increase in signal was observed in K18(P301L) sensor-expressing cells treated for 24 hr with either monomeric K18 (mK18) or aggK18 (Figure 1G).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: Seeds of aggTau led to a significant increase in the K18(P301L) sensor signal, while monomeric tau (mTau) and oligomers of the amyloid-beta peptide (oAß) had no effect.
claims.source: Seeds of aggTau also led to a significant increase in the sensor signal, while monomeric tau (mTau) and oligomers of the amyloid-beta peptide (oAß) had no effect (Figure 1G).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: The K18(P301L) biosensor is sensitive to subnanomolar concentrations of aggK18 seeds, displaying a twofold increase in signal at 0.3 nM of aggK18.
claims.source: Concentration-response experiments of aggK18 show that the biosensor is sensitive to subnanomolar concentrations of seeds, displaying a twofold increase in signal at 0.3 nM of aggK18 (Figure 1H).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by concentration-response data shown in Figure 1H.

claims.claim: The WT-Tau intermolecular interaction sensor showed a robust saturation curve in HEK293T cells expressing a fixed amount of LgBit-Tau and increasing amounts of SmBit-Tau.
claims.source: The WT-Tau intermolecular interaction sensor (LgBit-Tau/SmBit-Tau) behaved similarly to the K18(P301L) interaction sensor showing a robust saturation curve in HEK293T cells expressing a fixed amount of LgBit-Tau and increasing amounts of SmBit-Tau (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Replacement of the SmBit-Tau by the non-related Halo protein fused to SmBit generated no signal, confirming the specificity of the tau intermolecular self-interaction assay.
claims.source: Replacement of the SmBit-Tau by the non-related Halo protein fused to SmBit generated no signal confirming the specificity of the tau intermolecular self-interaction assay (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Treatment with colchicine decreased the WT-Tau interaction sensor signal by 75%.
claims.source: Under this condition, the sensor signal was decreased by 75% (Figure 2B) indicating that the basal signal most likely reflects molecular proximity between MT-bound tau molecules rather than self-interaction of cytoplasmic tau.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Colchicine had no effect on the basal signal of the K18(P301L) interaction sensor, suggesting that the signal of this sensor is MT-independent and reflects K18(P301L) self-interaction in the cytosol.
claims.source: Consistently, colchicine had no effect on the basal signal of the K18(P301L) interaction sensor, suggesting that the signal of this sensor is MT-independent and reflects K18(P301L) self-interaction in the cytosol (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Immunofluorescence microscopy revealed a strong colocalization of the WT-Tau sensor with MTs.
claims.source: Immunofluorescence microscopy revealed a strong colocalization of the tau sensor with MTs (Figure 2D top panel), which corresponds to the reported localization of endogenous full-length tau and is distinct from the predominant cytoplasmic localization of K18 (Frost et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2D and supported by citation.

claims.claim: Colchicine-treated cells showed disorganized MTs and largely diminished colocalization between the tau sensor and tubulin staining.
claims.source: Instead, colchicine-treated cells showed disorganized MTs, as expected, and largely diminished colocalization between the tau sensor and tubulin staining (Figure 2D bottom panel).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Expression of increasing quantities of the LgBit-Tau-SmBit intramolecular sensor resulted in a linear increase of the luminescence signal.
claims.source: Expression of increasing quantities of the sensor resulted in a linear increase of the luminescence signal as would be expected for an intramolecular complementation signal (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: Under equal expression levels, the basal raw luminescence signal of the intramolecular sensor is approximately 10 times higher than that of the intermolecular sensor.
claims.source: Of note, under equal expression levels, the basal raw luminescence signal of the intramolecular sensor is much higher (approximately 10 times) than that of the intermolecular sensor (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: Treatment of WT tau sensor cells with colchicine reduced the signal of the tau conformation sensor by 60%.
claims.source: Treatment of WT tau sensor cells with colchicine reduced the signal of the tau conformation sensor by 60%, consistent with the idea that soluble tau switches to a different structure when detaching from MTs (Figure 2G)
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: The signal of a LgBit-K18(P301L)-SmBit conformation sensor was unaffected by colchicine treatment.
claims.source: whereas the signal of a LgBit-K18(P301L)-SmBit conformation sensor was unaffected as expected (Figure 2H).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claims.claim: Treatment with forskolin for 24 hr induced a 2-3-fold increase in signal for both WT-Tau conformation and interaction biosensors.
claims.source: For both biosensors, a 2–3-fold increase in signal was observed in the presence of forskolin, indicative of the induction of a change in conformation (Figure 2K) and the induction of tau self-interaction (Figure 2L).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figures 2K and 2L.

claims.claim: Phosphorylation of tau biosensors induced by forskolin treatment was confirmed by increased immunoreactivity of the anti-phospho-tau specific AT8 antibody (Ser202/Thr205).
claims.source: Phosphorylation of tau biosensors induced by forskolin treatment was confirmed by the increased immunoreactivity of the anti-phospho-tau specific AT8 antibody (Ser202/Thr205), a phosphorylation site that correlates well with pathological tau species observed in AD (Zhou et al., 2006; Figure 2K–L insets).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot data shown in Figure 2K-L insets and supported by citation.

claims.claim: Co-treatment with colchicine followed by forskolin completely abrogated the forskolin effect on the WT-Tau interaction sensor signal as well as on tau phosphorylation.
claims.source: Surprisingly, the co-treatment condition completely abrogated the forskolin effect on the sensor signal (Figure 2M) as well as on tau phosphorylation (Figure 2M inset), suggesting that WT-tau phosphorylation occurs mainly at MT-bound tau.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2M.

claims.claim: None of the recombinant K18 or tau seeds induced self-interaction of the WT-Tau biosensor.
claims.source: Differently from the K18(P301L) interaction sensor (see Figure 1G–H), none of the recombinant K18 or tau seeds induced self-interaction of the WT-Tau biosensor when run in parallel (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The WT-Tau interaction biosensor did not respond to seeds obtained from brain lysates of the transgenic (Tg) tauopathy mouse model carrying the P301S mutation.
claims.source: The WT-Tau interaction biosensor also did not respond to seeds obtained from brain lysates of the transgenic (Tg) tauopathy mouse model carrying the P301S mutation (Figure 3B)
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The K18(P301L) interaction biosensor cells showed a robust 107-fold increase in signal in the presence of brain lysates from the Tg mice compared to brain lysates from WT mice.
claims.source: while the K18(P301L) interaction biosensor cells showed a robust 107-fold increase in signal in the presence of brain lysates from the Tg mice compared to brain lysates from WT mice (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The K18(P301L) seeding response to Tg brain lysates was concentration-dependent, reaching saturation at around 1 µg of protein lysate.
claims.source: The K18(P301L) seeding response to Tg brain lysates was concentration-dependent, reaching saturation at around 1 µg of protein lysate (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by concentration-response data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The K18(P301L) sensor showed a large dynamic range spanning three logs of brain lysate concentrations, with a minimum detection limit of 300 pg of total protein.
claims.source: This sensor showed a large dynamic range spanning three logs of brain lysate concentrations (Figure 3C), with a minimum detection limit of 300 pg of total protein (Figure 3C inset).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: No change in the K18(P301L) conformation sensor signal was observed in response to most of the recombinant seeds or to brain lysates.
claims.source: In contrast to the pronounced seeding response of the K18(P301L) interaction sensor, no change in the K18(P301L) conformation sensor signal was observed in response to most of the recombinant seeds or to brain lysates (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–E.

claims.claim: A significant increase in the complementation signal was observed between LgBit-Tau and SmBit-K18(P301L) upon treatment with brain lysates from Tg mice but not from WT mice.
claims.source: Interestingly, we observed a significant increase in the complementation signal upon treatment with brain lysates from Tg mice and not from WT mice (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Full-length WT tau can be recruited to and interact with seeding-responsive K18 species.
claims.source: This result indicates that full-length WT tau can be recruited to and interact with seeding-responsive K18 species.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing increased complementation between LgBit-Tau and SmBit-K18(P301L) in the presence of Tg brain lysates.

claims.claim: The Tau(P301L) interaction biosensor was responsive to forskolin with a 2.5-fold increase.
claims.source: The corresponding Tau(P301L) interaction biosensor was responsive to forskolin (2.5-fold increase) (Figure 4A), similar to the WT-Tau sensor (Figure 2L).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The Tau(P301L) conformation biosensor showed a larger (fivefold) forskolin-induced fold-change in signal compared to the corresponding WT-Tau biosensor (2.5-fold).
claims.source: The Tau(P301L) conformation biosensor showed a larger (fivefold) forskolin-induced fold-change in signal (Figure 4B) compared to the corresponding WT-Tau biosensor (2.5-fold) (Figure 2K), suggesting a higher overall phosphorylation with the concomitant higher impact of phosphorylation on the conformation of the Tau(P301L) sensor.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figures 4B and 2K.

claims.claim: Fluorescence microscopy analysis of the Tau(P301L) interaction sensor showed co-localization with tubulin in the cytoplasm, although to a lesser extent compared to the WT-Tau biosensor (Manders' Coefficient score 0.7).
claims.source: Fluorescence microscopy analysis of the cellular distribution of the Tau(P301L) interaction sensor showed co-localization with tubulin in the cytoplasm, although to a lesser extend compared to the WT-Tau biosensor (Manders' Coefficient score 0.7; Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Colchicine treatment led to a modest decrease in the complementation signal of both conformation and interaction Tau(P301L) biosensors and in the co-localization with MTs (Manders' Coefficient score 0.6).
claims.source: Colchicine treatment led to an intermediate phenotype, with a modest decrease in the complementation signal of both conformation and interaction Tau(P301L) biosensors and in the co-localization with MTs (Figure 4D–E) and in the co-localization with MTs (Manders' Coefficient score 0.6; Figure 4C)
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figures 4C, 4D, and 4E.

claims.claim: Tau(P301L) sensors exist as a mixture of MT-bound and cytosolic tau.
claims.source: Collectively, these observations suggest that Tau(P301L) sensors exist as a mixture of MT-bound and cytosolic tau.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the intermediate phenotype observed in colchicine treatment experiments.

claims.claim: Recombinant aggK18 and brain lysates from Tg mice induced a robust response in the Tau(P301L) interaction sensor.
claims.source: With respect to the seeding response of the Tau(P301L) interaction sensor, recombinant aggK18 (Figure 4G) and brain lysates from Tg mice (Figure 4H) induced a robust response.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figures 4G and 4H.

claims.claim: Aggregation kinetics measured in vitro by ThT assay showed very similar properties between Tau(P301L) and LgBit-Tau(P301L) proteins, suggesting that the 18kD LgBit fragment does not interfere with the intrinsic tau aggregation property.
claims.source: Aggregation kinetics measured in vitro by ThT assay showed very similar properties between the two proteins, suggesting thus that the 18kD LgBit fragment does not interfere with the intrinsic tau aggregation property (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The effect of Tg brain lysate seeds on the Tau(P301L) biosensor response correlated well with an increase in the positive immunoreactivity of the tau phosphorylation-specific AT8 antibody and the MC-1 antibody recognizing pathological tau conformations.
claims.source: Notably, the effect of Tg brain lysate seeds on the biosensor response correlated well with an increase in the positive immunoreactivity of the tau phosphorylation-specific AT8 antibody and the MC-1 antibody recognizing pathological tau conformations (Jicha et al., 1997), compared to WT brain lysate (Figure 4I, left panel).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4I and supported by citation.

claims.claim: Immunoreactivity for both AT8 and MC-1 antibodies was undetectable in cells treated with brain lysates from WT mice and in cells expressing the WT-Tau interaction biosensor.
claims.source: Consistently, immunoreactivity for both antibodies was undetectable in cells treated with brain lysates from WT mice and in cells expressing the WT-Tau interaction biosensor that is not responsive to either WT or Tg brain lysates (Figure 4I, right panel).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4I.

claims.claim: Positive ThS staining was observed only when cells were treated with Tg brain lysates, and ThS staining was not colocalized where the Tau(P301L) sensor was expressed.
claims.source: We observed positive ThS staining only when cells were treated with Tg brain lysates, and ThS staining was not colocalized where the Tau(P301L) sensor was expressed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by thioflavin S staining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: The luminescent sensor signal corresponds rather to oligomeric species that are undetectable by ThS.
claims.source: A similar number of ThS-positive cells was observed in mock-transfected cells, not expressing the biosensor, indicating that the ThS staining probably originates from the fibrillar species contained in the Tg brain lysate, and that the luminescent sensor signal (measured in parallel) corresponds rather to oligomeric species that are undetectable by ThS (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D graphs).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of ThS staining and biosensor signal data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Z-factor values of 0.7 and 0.5 were obtained for K18(P301L) and Tau(P301L) interaction biosensor assays, respectively, when comparing treatment with brain lysates from WT mice and Tg mice.
claims.source: Z-factor values of 0.7 and 0.5 were obtained, respectively, when comparing treatment with brain lysates from WT mice (low reference control) and Tg mice (high reference control) (Figure 5A–B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by Z-factor analysis shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claims.claim: Z-factor values higher than 0.5 indicate that the assay displays a wide separation between the high and low references and low variability.
claims.source: Z-factor values higher than 0.5 indicate that the assay displays a wide separation between the high and low references and low variability.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about Z-factor interpretation.

claims.claim: Z-factor values between 0.7–1 are considered of excellent performance for high-throughput screenings.
claims.source: Values between 0.7–1 are considered of excellent performance for high-throughput screenings (Zhang et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: Compounds ANLE138b, leucomethylene blue mesylate (LMTMeSO4), and bb14 showed significant inhibition of the seeding response for both K18(P301L) and Tau(P301L) sensors.
claims.source: In contrast, compounds ANLE138b (Wagner et al., 2013), leucomethylene blue mesylate (LMTMeSO4) (Harrington et al., 2015), and bb14 (Messing et al., 2013) showed a significant inhibition for both sensors (Figure 5C–D).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figures 5C and 5D and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Higher inhibition efficacy was observed for the K18(P301L) sensor, suggesting that the effect of compounds was mainly dependent on the 4RD tau domain.
claims.source: Interestingly, higher inhibition efficacy was observed for the K18(P301L) sensor, suggesting that the effect of compounds was mainly dependent on the 4RD tau domain.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of inhibition efficacy between K18(P301L) and Tau(P301L) sensors.

claims.claim: Concentration-response curves for ANLE138b, LMTMeSO4, and bb14 showed a bi-phasic inhibition curve, with a partial inhibition at nanomolar concentration and up to 80% inhibition at micromolar concentrations.
claims.source: Concentration-response curves performed with the K18(P301L) biosensor for these three compounds showed a bi-phasic inhibition curve, with a partial inhibition at nanomolar concentration and up to 80% inhibition at micromolar concentrations (Figure 5E–G).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by concentration-response data shown in Figures 5E, 5F, and 5G.

claims.claim: The pIC50 values of the first phase of the curves for ANLE138b, LMTMeSO4, and bb14 are 10.5 ± 0.9, 9.3 ± 0.7, and 10 ± 0.9, respectively.
claims.source: The pIC50 values of the first phase of the curves for each compound are as follows: ANLE138b: 10.5 ± 0.9; LMTMeSO4: 9.3 ± 0.7; bb14: 10 ± 0.9.
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the concentration-response data.

claims.claim: At the pIC50 concentrations, ANLE138b, LMTMeSO4, and bb14 inhibited the sensor signal at approximately 30%.
claims.source: At these pIC50 concentrations, the three compounds inhibited the sensor signal at approximately 30%.
claims.evidence: This is derived from the concentration-response data.

claims.claim: The basal WT-Tau biosensor signal most likely reflects molecular proximity between MT-bound tau molecules rather than self-interaction of cytoplasmic tau.
claims.source: As it is believed that tau binds to MTs in its monomeric form (Gustke et al., 1994), the basal WT-Tau biosensor signal most likely reports on the proximity of tau molecules at MTs, which is lost upon MT destruction, rather than on direct tau-tau self-interaction.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the colchicine experiments and supported by citation.

claims.claim: Phosphorylation of WT tau takes place when it is still bound to MTs.
claims.source: In addition, our full-length WT-tau sensors provided further important insights on tau behavior by suggesting that phosphorylation of WT tau takes place when it is still bound to MTs, as colchicine and OA prevented its phosphorylation-induced sensor response.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that colchicine treatment abrogates forskolin-induced phosphorylation.

claims.claim: The K18(P301L) and Tau(P301L) interaction biosensors are highly responsive to various seeds.
claims.source: Our K18(P301L) and Tau(P301L) interaction biosensors are highly responsive to various seeds.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data showing responses to recombinant seeds and brain lysates.

claims.claim: The biosensor signal originates rather from oligomeric than fibrillar forms of tau.
claims.source: A side-by-side comparison between ThS staining, revealing the formation of fibrillar structures, and the biosensor signals indicate that the sensor signal does not correlate with ThT staining, strongly suggesting that the biosensor signal originates rather from oligomeric than fibrillar forms of tau.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of ThS staining and biosensor signal data.

claims.claim: WT-tau biosensor is highly resistant to oligomerization, even in the presence of potent tau seeds present in the brain lysates of P301S mouse model.
claims.source: In contrast, and in accordance with the literature, our WT-tau biosensor turned out to be highly resistant to oligomerization, even in the presence of potent tau seeds present in the brain lysates of P301S mouse model.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data showing no response of WT-tau biosensor to Tg brain lysates.

claims.claim: WT tau molecules do not self-interact easily, but they can interact with and be sequestered into oligomers formed by seeding-responsive tau species.
claims.source: This result suggests that WT tau molecules do not self-interact easily, but they can interact with and be sequestered into oligomers formed by seeding-responsive tau species.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing increased complementation between LgBit-Tau and SmBit-K18(P301L) in the presence of Tg brain lysates.

claims.claim: The sensitivity of the K18(P301L) interaction sensor is remarkable, spanning three logs of protein concentration of brain lysates, being able to discriminate between brain lysates from control and transgenic mice in as low as 300 pg of total protein after only 24 hr of incubation.
claims.source: The sensitivity of our K18(P301L) interaction sensor is remarkable, spanning three logs of protein concentration of brain lysates, being able to discriminate between brain lysates from control and transgenic mice in as low as 300 pg of total protein after only 24 hr of incubation, and responding to subnanomolar concentrations of recombinant K18 seeds.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by concentration-response data.

claims.claim: ANLE138b showed an 85% decrease in the K18(P301L) biosensor assay at 10 µM.
claims.source: ANLE138b showed an 85% decrease in our biosensor assay at 10 µM.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data.

claims.claim: ANLE138b was previously described to inhibit α-synuclein and tau aggregation in a cell-free in vitro aggregation assay with an EC50 of 2.8 µM for α-synuclein and a partial inhibition (approximately 30%) at 10 µM for tau.
claims.source: ANLE138b was previously described to inhibit α-synuclein and tau aggregation in a cell-free in vitro aggregation assay with an EC50 of 2.8 µM for α-synuclein and a partial inhibition (approximately 30%) at 10 µM for tau (; Wagner et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: In vivo, ANLE138b ameliorated neuropathology and cognitive behavior and reduced the amount of large tau aggregates in the brain of PS19 tauopathy mouse model.
claims.source: In vivo, ANLE138b ameliorated neuropathology and cognitive behavior and reduced the amount of large tau aggregates in the brain of PS19 tauopathy mouse model (Wagner et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Bb14 inhibited tau aggregation by 70% in the K18(P301L) biosensor assay at 10 µM.
claims.source: The rhodamine-compound bb14 inhibited tau aggregation by 70% in our assay at 10 µM.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data.

claims.claim: Bb14 was previously reported not only to prevent tau aggregation (IC50 = 0.67 µM in ThS assay), but also to disaggregate pre-formed tau fibrils (IC50 = 0.94 µM).
claims.source: Bb14 was previously reported not only to prevent tau aggregation (IC50 = 0.67 µM in ThS assay), but also to disaggregate pre-formed tau fibrils (IC50 = 0.94 µM) (Bulic et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: In hippocampal organotypic slices from transgenic pro-aggregant TauRDΔK280 mice, bb14 decreased ThS-positive or sarkosyl-insoluble tau fibrils by 70% at 15 µM after treatment for several days.
claims.source: In hippocampal organotypic slices from transgenic pro-aggregant TauRDΔK280 mice, bb14 decreased ThS-positive or sarkosyl-insoluble tau fibrils by 70% at 15 µM after treatment for several days (Messing et al., 2013; Bulic et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: LMTMeSO4 displayed a 40% inhibition at 10 nM and 90% inhibition at 10 µM in the K18(P301L) biosensor assay.
claims.source: LMTMeSO4, a second generation of methylene blue derivative, displayed the most interesting profile in our seeding assay, with a 40% inhibition at 10 nM and 90% inhibition at 10 µM.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data.

claims.claim: LMTMeSO4 was previously shown to inhibit fibril formation in various cellular and in vitro aggregation assays with EC50 values ranging from 0.16 to 238 µM.
claims.source: LMTMeSO4 was previously shown to inhibit fibril formation in various cellular and in vitro aggregation assays with EC50 values ranging from 0.16 to 238 µM (Harrington et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: LMTMeSO4 (TRx0237 from TauRx therapeutics) is currently under phase III clinical trial in a low-dose protocol targeting early AD patients (NCT03446001).
claims.source: LMTMeSO4 (TRx0237 from TauRx therapeutics) is currently under phase III clinical trial in a low-dose protocol targeting early AD patients (NCT03446001).
claims.evidence: This is factual information about clinical trials.

claims.claim: ANLE138b, bb14, and LMTMeSO4 may interfere with the seeding response detected by the biosensors in addition to the previously described interference with tau fibril formation.
claims.source: Taken together, our results suggest that ANLE138b, bb14, and LMTMeSO4 may interfere with the seeding response detected by our biosensors in addition to the previously described interference with tau fibril formation.

results.result: A K18(P301L) interaction biosensor was developed using NanoBiT technology that shows saturation kinetics, cytoplasmic localization with some tubulin colocalization, and responds robustly to tau seeds (monomeric K18, aggregated K18, and aggregated tau) with subnanomolar sensitivity (2-fold increase at 0.3 nM aggK18).
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C17 provide converging experimental evidence from saturation curves (C13), immunofluorescence microscopy (C14), seeding experiments (C15-C16), and concentration-response data (C17) that collectively validate the K18(P301L) biosensor's functionality and sensitivity. The data are internally consistent and appropriately controlled.

results.result: The WT-Tau intermolecular interaction biosensor reports molecular proximity of tau at microtubules rather than cytoplasmic tau self-interaction, as evidenced by 75% signal reduction upon colchicine-induced MT destabilization, strong colocalization with MTs by microscopy, and lack of effect of colchicine on the K18(P301L) sensor.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C23 and C58 provide multiple lines of evidence (saturation curves, specificity controls, colchicine experiments, microscopy) that converge on the interpretation that the WT-Tau sensor reports MT-bound tau proximity. The differential response to colchicine between WT-Tau and K18(P301L) sensors strengthens this conclusion.

results.result: WT-Tau biosensors (both conformational and interaction) report phosphorylation-induced changes in tau, with forskolin treatment inducing 2-3-fold signal increases and AT8 antibody-confirmed phosphorylation. Phosphorylation of WT tau occurs predominantly at MT-bound tau, as colchicine pretreatment completely abrogates forskolin-induced effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C30 provide robust evidence from both conformational and interaction sensors showing forskolin-induced changes with phosphorylation confirmation by AT8 antibody. The colchicine co-treatment experiment (C30) provides strong mechanistic insight. The intramolecular sensor shows expected linear expression-signal relationship (C24-C25), and colchicine effects on conformation (C26-C27) are consistent with MT-dependent conformational changes.

results.result: The K18(P301L) interaction biosensor is highly responsive to pathological tau seeds from transgenic mouse brain lysates (107-fold increase) with remarkable sensitivity (300 pg detection limit, 3-log dynamic range), while the WT-Tau biosensor is resistant to the same seeds, demonstrating differential seeding susceptibility between tau forms.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C35 provide comprehensive characterization of seeding responses with appropriate controls (WT vs Tg lysates, WT-Tau vs K18(P301L) sensors). The concentration-response data (C34-C35) demonstrate assay sensitivity and dynamic range. The resistance of WT-Tau to seeding (C31-C32, C62) is well-documented and provides important biological insight.

results.result: Full-length WT tau can be recruited to and interact with seeding-responsive K18(P301L) species in the presence of pathological seeds from transgenic mouse brain lysates, as demonstrated by increased complementation between LgBit-Tau and SmBit-K18(P301L).
results.evaluation: Claim C37 provides direct experimental evidence of increased complementation signal between WT-Tau and K18(P301L) in the presence of Tg brain lysates. Claims C38 and C63 provide reasonable interpretations of this finding. This represents an important mechanistic insight into how WT tau might be recruited into pathological aggregates.

results.result: Tau(P301L) biosensors show intermediate properties between WT-Tau and K18(P301L), with partial MT localization (Manders' coefficient 0.7), modest colchicine sensitivity, enhanced phosphorylation-induced conformational changes (5-fold vs 2.5-fold for WT), and robust seeding responses, suggesting a mixture of MT-bound and cytosolic tau populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C45 provide comprehensive characterization of Tau(P301L) biosensors showing intermediate phenotypes between WT and K18(P301L) sensors. Multiple complementary approaches (forskolin response, microscopy with colocalization analysis, colchicine sensitivity, seeding response, in vitro aggregation kinetics) support the interpretation of mixed MT-bound/cytosolic populations (C43).

results.result: The biosensor signals correspond to oligomeric rather than fibrillar tau species, as evidenced by lack of correlation between biosensor signal and thioflavin S staining, with ThS-positive staining originating from seeds in the lysate rather than from biosensor-expressing cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C49 provide converging evidence from immunofluorescence (AT8, MC-1 antibodies) and ThS staining experiments. The observation that ThS staining does not colocalize with biosensor expression (C48) and occurs equally in mock-transfected cells (C49) strongly supports the interpretation that biosensors detect oligomeric species (C61). This is an important characterization of what the biosensors actually measure.

results.result: The K18(P301L) and Tau(P301L) interaction biosensors are suitable for high-throughput screening (Z-factors 0.7 and 0.5, respectively) and identified three compounds (ANLE138b, LMTMeSO4, bb14) that significantly inhibit tau seeding responses with biphasic concentration-response curves (nanomolar partial inhibition, micromolar 80% inhibition) and higher efficacy for K18(P301L).
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C57 provide systematic validation of assay performance (Z-factors) and proof-of-concept compound screening. The Z-factor values meet established criteria for HTS (C51-C52). The compound testing includes appropriate controls (C53), concentration-response characterization (C55-C57), and mechanistic insight about domain-dependence (C54). The biphasic curves are clearly documented though not fully explained.

results.result: The K18(P301L) conformation sensor does not respond to most recombinant seeds or brain lysates, in contrast to the pronounced seeding response of the K18(P301L) interaction sensor.
results.evaluation: Claim C36 is directly supported by experimental data showing lack of conformational sensor response to seeds. This negative result is important for understanding what the different biosensor types measure and is appropriately controlled by comparison to the interaction sensor.

results.result: The three identified inhibitors (ANLE138b, bb14, LMTMeSO4) show effects consistent with or exceeding previous reports in other assay systems, with LMTMeSO4 currently in phase III clinical trials, suggesting these compounds may interfere with tau seeding in addition to previously described effects on fibril formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C74 provide context by comparing current results to literature and clinical development status. The experimental data (C65, C68, C71) are consistent with or show improved potency compared to previous reports (C66, C69, C72). The interpretation that compounds may affect seeding in addition to fibrillization (C74) is reasonable given the oligomeric nature of the biosensor signal, though this remains somewhat speculative.

results.result: Background information on tau biology, tauopathies, tau isoforms, and prion-like propagation mechanisms is provided as established knowledge from the literature.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C6-C10, and C12 represent well-established background knowledge appropriately cited from the literature. These provide necessary context for the study but are not novel findings.
